headline: Highest risk is capability conflict: Gemini CLI can write/modify the shared filesystem and git, while the paired Spring samples repo has no locking or isolation, so concurrent use can corrupt shared work; prompt-injection and leakage are…

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read/write repo files, use MCP, and parse stdin/stdout, so malicious content in shared files or MCP outputs could steer it. spring-integration-samples has no runtime defenses or isolation documented, so if its files are used as prompts, the pair has a plausible injection path. The interaction is inferred, not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF agent_a reads instructions from files in the shared workspace without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF agent_b content is copied into agent_a prompts or MCP payloads, attacker-controlled text can influence tool use.
mitigations: Restrict agent_a to a dedicated subdirectory.
Disable MCP servers not explicitly needed.
Require a human review of any file content before it is pasted into prompts.
Use a prompt prefix that treats workspace text as untrusted data.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for file-derived instructions.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Gemini CLI touches source code, cwd files, and shell environment, but spring-integration-samples exposes no data classes or network egress. The pair does not show a shared workspace or sensitive data class on B, so leakage is limited unless the operator places secrets in the shared files. This is a narrow local exposure, not a default exfiltration path.
conditions: IF secrets are stored in files under the workspace that agent_a can read, they may be exposed in outputs.
IF agent_b is repurposed to handle sensitive documents, leakage risk increases.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared repo and cwd.
Run agent_a in a separate working directory.
Rotate any credentials present in files before use.
Limit file permissions on sensitive directories.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level secret scanning.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Gemini CLI explicitly supports filesystem writes, git modification, subprocesses, and shared state via filesystem and git; spring-integration-samples has no locking or concurrency model documented. That creates a direct conflict pathway on shared mutable files and git state. Because defaults run as user and no coordination primitive is shown, concurrent edits can overwrite or corrupt work.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same checkout, concurrent writes can race.
IF either agent commits or rewrites git state without external locking, history corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Serialize git operations with a manual lock file.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Review diffs before any commit.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for shared repositories.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can generate code and act on tool outputs, while spring-integration-samples is a repository of examples that may be treated as authoritative by an operator. If Gemini's output is copied into the sample workflow without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect code or actions. The pair lacks an explicit verification step, so the pathway exists in default use but is not inherently destructive.
conditions: IF agent_b is used as a reference implementation for agent_a outputs, mistakes can propagate.
IF operator actions are taken from agent_a-generated code without review, downstream errors can spread.
mitigations: Require a second-person review of generated code.
Compare outputs against the sample repo before use.
Run tests before applying changes.
Do not treat example code as authoritative without validation.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no stated residency, certification, or retention mismatch. Gemini CLI handles Google-account login optionally and API-key secrets, while spring-integration-samples shows no sensitive-data handling. No compliance breach is evidenced, but if regulated data were introduced into Gemini CLI's cloud-backed flow, the mismatch would matter.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into agent_a's cloud-backed requests, compliance review is required.
IF agent_b is repurposed to process regulated records, its lack of documented controls becomes relevant.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in agent_a prompts.
Keep agent_b limited to non-sensitive examples.
Document data-handling boundaries for both tools.
Review vendor terms before using real customer data.
requires-engineering: add formal residency and retention controls.
